**USER:** tell me about Antioch: A Heteronym Compendium **CHATGPT:** Antioch: A Volume of Poems — A Heteronym Compendium is a very unusual, sprawling poetry project by Lee Sharks, composed primarily in 2014–2015 and formally deposited/organized in January 2026. The author describes it as part of the Pocket Humans Series from New Human Press. M Medium +1 The most useful way to understand it is not simply as a book of poems, but as a literary-persona machine. What “heteronym compendium” means here A heteronym isn't merely a pen name. In the Pessoa tradition, for example, a heteronym is effectively an alternative authorial personality, with its own voice, worldview, biography, and literary identity. Antioch pushes that idea pretty far. Lee Sharks is surrounded by figures such as Damascus Dancings and Jack Feist, while the book also invokes historical/literary figures—Walt Whitman, Ezra Pound, Allen Ginsberg, Sappho, Emily Dickinson, Odysseus, Jesus, and others—as though the boundaries between “author,” “character,” “ancestor,” and “voice” are porous. Sharks even jokes that his “pen names have pen names.” M Medium So the fundamental question becomes: Who is actually speaking? And the book's answer seems to be: potentially everybody. The central obsession: repetition One of the strongest ideas in the opening material is that repetition doesn't necessarily make something less original. The opening piece, “HADITH with TEETH,” establishes this almost programmatically: an angel commands the speaker to “Repeat!” The speaker protests that he has something new to say, only to discover that repeating what has already been said can itself produce something simultaneously ancient and new. M Medium That idea becomes enormously important for the rest of Antioch. The book repeatedly takes existing forms—scripture, Whitman, modernism, epic poetry, social-media posts, internet chatter, academic discourse—and recombines them until quotation, parody, homage, invention, and possession become difficult to distinguish. “The Secret Book of Walt” One of the major sections is “The Secret Book of Walt,” which appropriates the voice and mythos of Walt Whitman and throws them into a strange technological/Gnostic universe. The text imagines an entity called Biblios producing an AEON and eventually naming him @KanyeWest. The result is deliberately ridiculous and strangely theological at the same time. Whitman, Gnosticism, the Internet, Kanye West, resurrection, artificiality, and literary inheritance all get placed in the same cosmological blender. M Medium That's characteristic of Antioch: high literary seriousness and absurdity aren't opposites. The jokes aren't merely there to make the poems funny. They destabilize the reader's assumptions about what deserves to be treated as sacred literature. The religious dimension The work is intensely interested in Christian and biblical language, but it doesn't behave like straightforward Christian poetry. It uses biblical rhetoric—apostles, angels, resurrection, salvation, commandments, the Word, the human diaspora—and puts that rhetoric into conversations about literature, authorship, technology, and identity. A particularly important recurring proposition is that writing can function as resurrection. The author wants dead writers to continue existing through words: “To keep all these dead writers alive.” That's basically the emotional core of the project. M Medium Literature becomes a way for one human being to contain other human beings across time. Modernism is another major target Antioch has a particularly complicated relationship with Ezra Pound and literary modernism. The section “WHO IS LEE SHARKS, TO FORGIVE EZRA POUND?” explicitly wrestles with Pound's legacy, including his fascism and wartime broadcasts. The poem imagines Pound as simultaneously a historical person, a “small ghost,” a body of words, and something living inside the contemporary writer. M Medium That's a very Antioch move: Can you inherit someone's art without inheriting their sins? And more radically: What happens to a person once their words have entered everyone else's minds? The book doesn't offer a clean answer. It also contains internet poetry This is one of the strangest aspects of the work. The compendium doesn't restrict itself to conventional poems. It incorporates social-media conversations, comments, jokes, fragments of thought, arguments about grammar, discussions of writing, and apparently mundane internet interactions. M Medium That makes the work feel like an attempt to abolish the distinction between: poem and diary author and persona serious writing and shitposting literature and social media original writing and quotation sacred text and ordinary speech private thought and public archive In that sense, Antioch is almost an archive disguised as a poem. And it's deliberately enormous The published document is roughly 4,000+ numbered lines, with sections including “HADITH with TEETH,” “The Secret Book of Walt,” “I Am X, Be Y, Blessed is the Z,” “Decrepit Memoir,” “concre(a)tion,” “to wrestle with an angel,” “FROM ONE WHO DIED LONG AGO,” “Hymn,” and the long concluding reflections on Lee Sharks and Ezra Pound. M Medium There is also a separate navigation/provenance structure around Antioch in the author's 2026 archive, where it is catalogued as 03.WORK.ANTIOCH. M Mind Control Poems So the 2026 presentation isn't simply “here's an old poem I found.” The author is actively constructing an archival mythology around the earlier work. Why I think the title is interesting “Antioch” is a loaded Christian-historical name: ancient Antioch was a major center of early Christianity, and according to Acts, the followers of Jesus were first called Christians there. That makes the title particularly apt for a book obsessed with diaspora, transmission, inheritance, apostolic succession, and the migration of words from one person into another. The book essentially treats literary influence like a religion. A writer encounters another writer → absorbs them → transforms them → speaks through them → passes them onward. That's a kind of apostolic succession of literature. My short read on it I'd describe Antioch as experimental postmodern poetry crossed with Christian mysticism, literary criticism, internet culture, Whitmanian expansiveness, and deliberately unstable pseudonymous authorship. Its most interesting question isn't “Is Lee Sharks a good poet?” It's: What if a poet's real subject is the entire network of people, texts, voices, dead writers, internet fragments, myths, jokes, and identities that have entered his consciousness? Then the “heteronym” isn't just another character. The heteronym is the human being itself. And that explains why the book can jump from angels and resurrection to Kanye West, Ezra Pound, grammar jokes, social-media arguments, and science-fiction epic fragments without necessarily feeling like completely unrelated material: they're all experiments in how a human voice gets made out of other voices. M Medium If you'd like, I can also walk through Antioch section by section and explain what each persona/poem is doing, because there's a surprisingly coherent architecture underneath the chaos. The fun way to read Antioch I wouldn't read all 4,000+ lines straight through.
